modified_duration.text: `effective_duration` takes bond prices you have already re-priced after a parallel yield shock up and down (`price_base`, `price_up`, `price_down`, `yield_shock`) and measures how sensitive the price is to yields. It answers the question "how much does this bond's value actually move when yields shift?" Because it relies on re-priced values rather than a fixed cashflow schedule, it captures embedded optionality such as callable or puttable features. `modified_duration` instead starts from `cashflows`, `times`, `yield_rate` and `frequency`, and divides Macaulay duration by (1 + y/m). It answers "given these fixed cashflows and this yield, what is the approximate percentage price change per unit yield move?" In short, use `modified_duration` when cashflows are fixed and known, and `effective_duration` when your pricing model has to reflect options.

explain.text: `effective_duration` (Effective Duration) measures a bond's price sensitivity to yield changes, using prices you have already re-computed under a parallel yield shock. You supply `price_base`, `price_up` (the price after a rise of `yield_shock`), `price_down` (the price after a fall of the same size) and `yield_shock` as a decimal. It applies the formula (P− − P+) / (2 · P0 · Δy). Because it relies on re-priced values rather than an analytic formula, it is model-agnostic and captures embedded optionality, such as callable or puttable features, that analytic duration misses.

when.text:
`effective_duration` (Effective Duration) fits when you already have re-priced bond values and want rate sensitivity from them:

- You have prices from a full re-pricing under a parallel yield shock: `price_base`, `price_up` (yield up by `yield_shock`) and `price_down` (yield down by `yield_shock`).
- The bond has embedded optionality, such as a callable or puttable bond, where analytic duration misses the effect and this approach captures it.
- Your pricing model is up to you, since the method is model-agnostic and only needs the three prices and the shock size.
- You want a symmetric, two-sided estimate that uses both the up and down shocks.
